title: Artificial Intelligence · Episode 1
chapters: Expert systems: when AI ran on rules
How AI learns: walking downhill in the fog

units.t: Artificial Intelligence. Episode one.
In this episode: A short history of AI, Expert systems: when AI ran on rules, How machines learn and How AI learns: walking downhill in the fog.
Part one. A short history of AI.
AI did not arrive overnight.
It is a 70-year story of bold promises, bitter winters and a few moments that stunned the world.
Turing and Dartmouth.
In 1950 the British mathematician Alan Turing, famous for wartime code-breaking, published 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', asking: can machines think?
Because 'thinking' is hard to define, he proposed the imitation game, now the Turing test.
If a judge chatting through text could not reliably tell a machine from a person, we should take its intelligence seriously.
He also predicted machines might one day learn, not just be programmed step by step.

The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined by John McCarthy in a proposal for a 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire, organised with Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and Nathaniel Rochester.
It produced no single breakthrough, but gave the field a name, a community and an ambitious agenda.
Early optimism.
The first decades of AI were dominated by symbolic AI: programs built from hand-written rules and logic.
They proved maths theorems, played draughts and solved puzzles.
In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA mimicked a therapist using simple pattern matching, and some users became emotionally attached to it, which alarmed its creator.
Confidence ran high.
In 1965 Herbert Simon predicted that within twenty years machines would be capable of doing any work a person can do.
Meanwhile, Frank Rosenblatt's 1958 perceptron, an early learning machine loosely inspired by brain cells, hinted at a different path that was largely sidelined for years.
The AI winters.
Real-world problems proved far messier than puzzles.
Programs that worked in tidy demonstrations failed on everyday language and vision, and computers were too slow and data too scarce.
In the early 1970s, critical reviews such as Britain's 1973 Lighthill report led governments to cut funding, beginning the first 'AI winter'.
The 1980s brought a boom in expert systems, rule-based programs that captured specialist knowledge for businesses.
They proved expensive and brittle, and by the late 1980s and early 1990s the market collapsed into a second winter.
The lesson: hype can outrun what the technology can actually do.
Deep Blue and deep learning.
In May 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov 3.
5 to 2.
5 in New York, after he had beaten an earlier version the year before.
Yet it did not learn as people do.
Specialised hardware evaluated around 200 million positions per second, combined with chess knowledge programmed by experts.
It was superb at chess and could do nothing else.
Learning machines never died.
Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio kept refining neural networks through the lean years.
By the 2010s huge internet datasets, fast graphics chips, GPUs, and better training methods had arrived.
In 2012 AlexNet, from Hinton's Toronto group, won the ImageNet image-recognition competition by a striking margin.
'Deep learning' soon transformed speech, translation and image analysis.
The trio shared the 2018 Turing Award.
AlphaGo to chatbots.
Go has vastly more positions than chess, so brute force alone could not master it.
In March 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo beat top professional Lee Sedol four games to one in Seoul.
It combined deep neural networks, search and reinforcement learning, improving partly by playing itself.
In game two it played Move 37, which experts first thought a mistake but later saw as brilliant.
Many had expected this milestone to be years away.
In 2017 Google researchers introduced the transformer, which made it practical to train on enormous amounts of text.
This led to large language models, and ChatGPT's release in November 2022 made them mainstream.
Past predictions were often wildly optimistic, yet deep learning has also surprised sceptics.
Treat confident forecasts in either direction with caution.
The key idea: In 1950 Turing proposed a conversation test of machine intelligence, and in 1956 the field was named.
Part two. Expert systems: when AI ran on rules.
In the 1980s, the future of AI was supposed to be computers stuffed with the knowledge of human experts.
Businesses spent fortunes on it.
Then the boom went bust.
Bottling expertise.
In the 1960s and 1970s, researchers such as Edward Feigenbaum at Stanford argued for dropping general problem-solvers and focusing on deep knowledge of one narrow field.

Interview human experts, write what they know as hundreds or thousands of rules, such as 'if the patient has a fever and a stiff neck, consider meningitis', and let an inference engine chain the rules together.
These programs became known as expert systems.
An early success was DENDRAL, begun at Stanford in 1965 with Feigenbaum, geneticist Joshua Lederberg and chemist Carl Djerassi.
It helped chemists work back from the fragments of mass spectrometry to a molecule's structure, ranking possible structures.
Some results appeared in scientific papers.
Its lesson: power came less from clever general reasoning than from specialised knowledge.
MYCIN explains itself.
In the 1970s Edward Shortliffe and colleagues at Stanford built MYCIN, which identified bacteria causing serious blood infections and recommended antibiotics.
Several hundred rules carried 'certainty factors', since medical evidence is rarely clear-cut.
In a formal evaluation, experts rated its advice as good as or better than that of infectious disease specialists.
Yet it was never used in hospitals, because of slow question sessions, the computers of the day and unresolved questions of responsibility if it was wrong.
Its strength was transparency.
Asked why it wanted to know something, MYCIN showed the rule it was applying; asked how it reached a conclusion, it listed the chain of rules.
Modern neural networks are far harder to interpret, so explainable AI researchers try to recover some of that clarity for medicine, lending and law.
The boom.
By the early 1980s, expert systems had left the laboratory.
A famous example was XCON, developed with Carnegie Mellon University for Digital Equipment Corporation.
It configured complex computer orders, working out which cables, cabinets and components a customer's system needed, a job that had produced costly errors.
XCON grew to thousands of rules, and the company estimated it saved tens of millions of dollars a year.
Such successes sparked a boom.

Companies set up AI departments, start-ups sold specialised hardware and software, and in 1982 Japan launched its ambitious Fifth Generation Computer project, prompting rival government programmes in Britain, Europe and the United States.
The knowledge bottleneck.
The trouble was getting knowledge in.
Experts often cannot fully explain what they do, because much of their skill is intuition built over years.
Interviewing them and turning their answers into rules was painstaking, a problem Feigenbaum called the knowledge acquisition bottleneck.
Systems also became hard to maintain, since a new rule could clash with existing ones in unexpected ways.
And they were brittle.
Step slightly outside the narrow domain, or give them a situation their rules did not anticipate, and they could fail badly, with no common sense to fall back on.
A medical rule system knew nothing about the world beyond its rules, not even that patients are people.
Bust and legacy.
By the late 1980s, expectations had run far ahead of results.
The market for specialised AI computers collapsed around 1987, as ordinary desktop machines became powerful enough to do the job more cheaply.
Funding was cut, companies folded, and the field entered what became known as the second AI winter.
Yet expert systems never disappeared.
Rule-based software still checks insurance claims, flags suspicious bank transactions, calculates tax and guides call centre staff, though rarely under the AI label.
Machine learning rose partly as an answer to the knowledge bottleneck: rather than asking experts to write down rules, let computers learn patterns directly from data.
The key idea: Expert systems captured a specialist's knowledge as if-then rules, and their power came from specialised knowledge rather than general reasoning.
Part three. How machines learn.
Nobody wrote the rules that let your phone recognise your face.
The machine worked them out from examples.
Here's how.
Learning from examples.
Traditional software follows rules a programmer writes by hand: if this, then that.
That suits payroll or calculators, but try writing rules to recognise a cat in a photo or tell spam from real email.
There are too many exceptions.
Machine learning takes a different approach.
You give the computer many examples and let it find the patterns itself.
Show a spam filter millions of emails marked 'spam' or 'not spam', and it learns which features, such as certain phrases, links or senders, tend to signal junk.
The result is called a model.
There are two stages.
Training is the learning phase: the model makes predictions, measures how wrong they are and adjusts, over and over.
Inference is using the finished model on new inputs.
Most models don't keep learning while you use them.
Supervised learning.
The most common kind of machine learning is supervised learning.
The training data comes with labels, the right answers.
To predict house prices, you might feed a model thousands of past sales with details like suburb, land size and bedrooms, along with what each sold for.
It learns how those features relate to price, then estimates prices for homes it has never seen.
The same approach powers medical image tools trained on scans labelled by specialists, and bank fraud detectors trained on transactions marked genuine or fraudulent.
The catch: good labels are slow and expensive to create, and the model can only be as good as they are.
Without labels.
Sometimes you have plenty of data but no labels.
Unsupervised learning looks for structure itself.
Clustering groups similar items: a supermarket might find distinct groups in loyalty card data, such as busy families or bargain hunters, without anyone defining them.
Anomaly detection spots things that don't fit, like an odd reading from a machine about to fail.
People still have to interpret the results.
Reinforcement learning works a bit like training a dog with treats.
An agent takes actions and gets rewards or penalties, learning which strategies earn the most reward.
AlphaGo improved by playing millions of games against itself.
Feedback from human raters helps make chatbots more helpful.
Designing the right reward is tricky: systems can find unexpected shortcuts.
Neural networks.
Many modern models are artificial neural networks, loosely inspired by the brain.
A network is made of layers of simple units, sometimes called neurons.
Each unit takes in numbers, weights them, adds them up and passes a result to the next layer.
The weights, the strength of each connection, are what the network learns.
During training, a method called backpropagation works out how each weight contributed to an error and nudges it slightly in a better direction.
Repeat that billions of times and useful patterns emerge.
'Deep' learning simply means networks with many layers.
Despite the name, they work very differently from real brains.
Overfitting and bias.
A student who memorises last year's exam answers aces the practice paper but fails when the questions change.
Models can do the same, called overfitting: fitting training data so closely, including its noise, that they do poorly on new examples.
Developers hold back a test set the model never sees and judge performance on that.
The goal is generalisation: working well in the real world.
A model also learns whatever its data shows, including past biases.
In 2018 Reuters reported that Amazon scrapped an experimental recruiting tool that penalised CVs mentioning women's activities, having learned from mostly male applicants.
Some facial analysis systems made more errors on darker-skinned faces, largely because of unrepresentative training photos.
When an automated system judges a loan, job application or medical image, ask what data it learned from and how it was tested.
The key idea: Machine learning finds patterns in data instead of following hand-written rules.
Part four. How AI learns: walking downhill in the fog.
Behind almost every modern AI lies one surprisingly simple idea: take a small step in the direction that makes your mistakes smaller, then repeat it billions of times.
Walking downhill in fog.
Imagine standing on a mountainside in dense fog.
You can't see the valley, but you want the lowest point.
So you feel the slope underfoot, step in the steepest downhill direction, and repeat.
This is gradient descent, the method used to train nearly all modern neural networks.
The mountain represents how wrong the model is, and each position is a different setting of its internal numbers.
To measure 'wrong', a model needs a loss function.
For house prices, it compares each prediction with the real price and combines the errors into one number.
For a language model, the loss measures how surprised it was by the actual next word.
The model becomes very good at whatever the loss measures, which isn't always exactly what we want.
Knobs and the gradient.
A neural network is controlled by parameters, also called weights, which you can picture as knobs.
A small model might have thousands; the largest today have billions or more.
Each combination of settings gives a different loss.
The gradient, a tool from calculus, tells you for every knob at once which way to turn it, and how strongly, to increase the loss fastest.
So you turn every knob a little the opposite way, lowering the loss slightly.
The French mathematician Augustin-Louis Cauchy described the method in 1847, long before computers.
What changed was the scale.
Choosing the step size.
How far should you step each time?
The learning rate controls it.
Too small, and training crawls.
Too large, and you overshoot the valley, leap up the opposite slope and may bounce around wildly or even climb higher, like taking giant strides on that foggy mountain.
Engineers spend a lot of effort tuning it.
A common practice is to start with larger steps and gradually shrink them, so the model can settle into a good spot.
Rough terrain, noisy steps.
Real loss landscapes are full of dips, ridges, plateaus and saddle points, which slope down in some directions and up in others.
In theory you could be trapped in a local minimum, a hollow far above the true lowest point.
In practice, very large networks seem to train well anyway: with millions of dimensions there is usually some direction still leading down, and many low points are roughly equally good.
Why it works so reliably is still being researched.
Checking every training example before each step would be painfully slow.
So training uses stochastic gradient descent: each step estimates the slope from a small random batch, perhaps a few hundred examples.
The path wobbles, but steps are quick, and the wobble can help avoid getting stuck.
Backpropagation's bookkeeping.
In a deep network with many layers, how do you work out how each of millions of weights contributed to the final error?
Backpropagation starts with the error at the output and works backwards, layer by layer, using the chain rule from calculus to share out responsibility for the mistake.
Several people developed versions of the idea, but a 1986 paper by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams made it widely known for training neural networks.
Backpropagation calculates the slope; gradient descent takes the step.
Repeated over enormous datasets, with clever variations, they are the engine of today's deep learning.
The key idea: Gradient descent trains a model by repeatedly stepping in the direction that shrinks its loss, the number measuring its mistakes.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What was the idea behind the Turing test?
Answer. A machine passes if a judge can't tell it from a person in chat.
Question two. Where did a system like DENDRAL get its power?
Answer. From specialised knowledge packed into it.
Question three. What is the key idea of machine learning?
Answer. The computer finds patterns from examples.
Question four. What does the loss function do?
Answer. It turns the model's errors into one number.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
